extracted.intended_audience: experimental scientists, students of scientific method, and practitioners learning quantitative induction and empirical data analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and practical principles for discovering, representing, interpolating, and extrapolating quantitative laws from experimental data, including graphical, algebraic, and theoretical methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use empirical formulae to represent data
rubrics_metrics.description: If we have a table containing certain values of a variable and the corresponding values of the variant, there are mathematical processes by which we can infallibly discover a mathematical formula yielding numbers in more or less exact agreement with the table.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume quantities will approximately conform to a law of the form y = A + Bx + Cx^2 (or higher powers as necessary). Select from the table as many points as there are constants to determine and solve for those constants. In many cases lower powers suffice; include higher powers only when needed. Example: Regnault's empirical formula for latent heat. Method of least squares may also be employed to obtain most probable constants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat empirical formulae as approximations, not natural laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical formulae do not coincide with natural laws; they are only approximations to the results of natural laws founded upon the general principles of approximation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical formulae give another function which within observational bounds yields nearly the same values, but do not reveal the precise nature of the true function. Beware of over-interpreting fitting success as proof of true law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three modes for discovering rational formulae
rubrics_metrics.description: There are perhaps three methods... (i) By purely haphazard trial. (2) By noting the general character of the variation of the quantities, and trying by preference functions which give a similar form of variation. (3) By deducing from previous knowledge the form of the function which is most likely to suit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Haphazard trial has low probability of success because the space of possible functions is vast. Better approaches rely on plotting (to see general character) and prior theoretical/analogical knowledge to narrow candidate functions. Even when a candidate is found, success is by deductive reasoning: showing the law gives the numbers, not vice versa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use theoretical and analogical reasoning to choose function form
rubrics_metrics.description: Theory and analogical reasoning must be our guides; the general nature of the phenomenon will often indicate the kind of law to be looked for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: direct simple proportion when one form of energy/substance converts to another; exponential form for cooling where previous effect influences ensuing effect; trigonometric functions when direction influences action; inverse square law for influences spreading through three-dimensional space. Relying on such considerations increases chances of finding the true law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply the Method of Least Squares for best-fit constants
rubrics_metrics.description: When a form of function has been correctly ascertained, the remaining work is mere mathematical computation... we may proceed by the Method of Least Squares to determine the most probable values as given by the whole of the experimental results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After selecting a candidate function and forming equations from selected data, if many data points exist use least squares to obtain the 'most probable' constants based on all measurements rather than only a subset.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graphical method: plot data and draw approximate curve
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare ruled paper, mark off values of the variable on the horizontal line, and mark a point for each corresponding value of the variant perpendicularly above it at height corresponding to the value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose scales so variations are conspicuous but not excessive. A curve drawn through points will show irregular inflections from errors; by drawing a line guided by a sense of continuity one can trace a curve that approximates the true law. Leave original marks so others can judge or redraw. Use engraved ruled paper or fine machine-ruled grids for greater accuracy; methods such as prick-through from one sheet to another can yield accurate blanks for presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust plotting scales and presentation pragmatically
rubrics_metrics.description: The exact scale of the drawing is not of much importance, but it may require to be adjusted according to circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different values may be attributed to the upright and horizontal divisions to make variations visible. When many curves are to be drawn, rule a good sheet and transfer points by pricking through to obtain accurate clean curves. Use a screw dividing engine for highest precision where available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use curves to infer class of functions and reduce trial space
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawing results in the form of a curve can help ascertain whether the curve is likely to return into itself, have infinite branches, be asymptotic, logarithmic, or trigonometric in character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seeing the curve's shape can indicate which classes of functions to try, narrowing haphazard trials. But if only a fragment of the curve is available, identification is uncertain because many curves can approximate each other locally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpolation requires theoretical laws for non-empirical certainty
rubrics_metrics.description: If the interpolation is to be more than empirical, we must have not only the experimental results, but the laws which they obey — we must in fact go through the complete process of scientific investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only when laws have been discovered and verified can interpolations be treated as secure. Common interpolation (without theory) is approximate and indeterminate; you must use a priori considerations (e.g., expect or exclude periodic fluctuations) to choose interpolation method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpolation by assuming simple polynomial character when justified
rubrics_metrics.description: Supposing that the phenomenon is non-periodic, we proceed to assume that the function can be expressed in a limited series of the powers of the variable. The number of powers which can be included depends upon the number of experimental results available, and must be at least one less than this number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., two experimental results -> assume straight line y = mx + n; three results -> assume parabola. Calculate coefficients algebraically; this is the common empirical approach to interpolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect polynomial degree by finite differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Take the differences between successive values, then the differences of those differences, and so on; if any series of differences approaches closely to zero it indicates the numbers may be represented by a finite empirical formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the nth differences are zero, the formula will contain only the first n − 1 powers of the variable. Use the calculus of differences or Lagrange/Thomson & Tait formulas for interpolation by differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: If differences don't vanish, consider non-polynomial laws (e.g., exponential)
rubrics_metrics.description: If no column of differences shows any tendency to become zero throughout, it is an indication that the law is of a more complicated, for instance of an exponential character, so that it requires different treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In such cases avoid forcing a polynomial fit; consider appropriate transforms or specialized interpolation methods. Dr J. Hopkinson's arithmetical interpolation is noted as a method intending to avoid arbitrariness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form equations from widely apart, nearly equidistant selected results
rubrics_metrics.description: Selecting some of our results widely apart and nearly equidistant, we form by means of them as many equations as there are constant quantities to be determined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solve these equations to get constants, then test the function against remaining data. If it fails, either select a new set of results to form equations or acknowledge function form was wrongly chosen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpolation vs extrapolation: be cautious extending beyond observed range
rubrics_metrics.description: To extend our inference far beyond the limits of experience is exceedingly unsafe. Our knowledge is at the best only approximate, and takes no account of small tendencies which may become great under extreme circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extrapolation is riskier than interpolation; without verified laws expect inaccuracies. Perform experiments under extreme conditions to test behaviour beyond ordinary ranges where small tendencies may amplify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent periodic variations with trigonometric (sine/cosine) series
rubrics_metrics.description: All periodic variations may be represented with any required degree of accuracy by formulas involving the sines and cosines of angles and their multiples; the form of any tidal or other wave may thus be expressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In meteorology three or four terms are usually sufficient. Use methods (e.g., Bessel's rule, least squares on Fourier terms) to calculate coefficients; these representations can often adequately capture periodic phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct interpretation when data represent areas or averages
rubrics_metrics.description: When numerical results correspond not to the height of single ordinates but to the area of the curve between two ordinates, or the average height between certain limits, simply plotting mean-point heights can be incorrect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply geometrical corrections (e.g., Lord Rayleigh's correction) to obtain close approximations to the true ordinates when measured quantities represent areas/averages rather than point values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat simple proportionality as provisionally true only
rubrics_metrics.description: Until reason to the contrary is shown, we should do well to look upon every law of simple proportion as only provisionally true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small portions of curves or crude measurements may disguise curvature; many phenomena only approximately follow direct proportion. Verify proportional laws and be prepared to replace them if higher-order effects become significant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer experiments under extreme conditions to test law robustness
rubrics_metrics.description: There is great importance in experiments in which we investigate the properties of substances under extreme circumstances of cold or heat, density or rarity, intense electric excitation, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because tendencies negligible in ordinary ranges may dominate under extremes, such experiments help reveal failures of empirical laws when extrapolated and help discover more general/rational laws.
